rules.name: Meteor Client — mod metadata
rules.description: A mod archive declares the mod id "meteor-client", the identifier used by Meteor Client.
rules.falsePositives: Very low. The mod id is declared by the client's own metadata. A third party could reuse the id, which is why the package-structure rule is evaluated independently and both are reported.
rules.limitations: Detects the archive on disk only. It does not prove the client was launched or used on a specific server; correlate with logs, Prefetch and memory findings.

rules.name: Meteor Client — class package structure
rules.description: A Java archive contains compiled classes under the package "meteordevelopment.meteorclient", which belongs to Meteor Client.
rules.falsePositives: Very low. Addons legitimately depend on these packages but do not ship them; a jar that contains the classes contains the client code.
rules.limitations: Renamed/re-obfuscated forks change package names and will not match. Detects presence on disk, not use.

rules.name: Meteor Client — classes loaded in a running JVM
rules.description: The internal class path of Meteor Client was found in the memory of a running Java (Minecraft) process, indicating its classes were loaded.
rules.falsePositives: Low. The string could be present if the user opened the client's jar in a Java-based tool running in the same JVM, which is uncommon for a game process.
rules.limitations: Only examines Java processes running at scan time. If the game was closed before the scan, no memory evidence exists.

rules.falsePositives: Addons may be cosmetic; review the addon's feature classes.
rules.limitations: An addon alone does nothing without Meteor Client; check for the client itself.

rules.name: Auto-clicker executed
rules.description: An executable whose name identifies it as an auto-clicker is stored inside the Minecraft instance. Auto-clickers automate attacks (CPS manipulation).
rules.falsePositives: Auto-clickers have non-gaming uses (accessibility, idle games). Execution time must be correlated with the game session.
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: DLL injector executed
rules.description: An executable named like a DLL injector is stored inside the Minecraft instance. Injectors are used to load ghost clients into the game process.
rules.falsePositives: Some modding tools for other games are named "injector".
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: Memory editor executed (Cheat Engine)
rules.description: Cheat Engine, a memory scanner/editor, is stored inside the Minecraft instance.
rules.falsePositives: Cheat Engine is commonly used for singleplayer games and learning.
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: Process manipulation tool executed
rules.description: Process Hacker / System Informer is stored inside the Minecraft instance. These tools can terminate processes, edit memory strings and unload modules.
rules.falsePositives: Popular legitimate administration tools.
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: Secure-delete tool executed
rules.description: A secure file deletion tool is stored inside the Minecraft instance. Secure deletion prevents recovery of files that were removed.
rules.falsePositives: Used legitimately for privacy.
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: Macro automation runtime executed (AutoHotkey)
rules.description: AutoHotkey is stored inside the Minecraft instance. AutoHotkey scripts can implement clicker or macro behaviour.
rules.falsePositives: AutoHotkey is a very common productivity tool.
rules.limitations: Matched against executables stored inside the selected instance. Names are user-controlled; a renamed tool will not match, but every executable in the instance is also string-scanned.

rules.name: File named after a known cheat client
rules.description: A Java archive, executable or library is named after a known cheat client.
rules.falsePositives: File names are user-controlled; a file may be mis-named, an installer, or unrelated. A name alone never confirms a client.
rules.limitations: Renamed clients will not match. The file content is analysed separately when it still exists.

rules.name: JNativeHook native library extracted
rules.description: The JNativeHook native library was extracted to a temporary folder. JNativeHook gives Java programs global mouse/keyboard hooks and is used by Java auto-clickers.
rules.falsePositives: Legitimate Java applications (hotkey tools, overlays) also use JNativeHook.
rules.limitations: Only observed in temporary folders; the extracting program is not identified.

rules.name: Unverified archive on the game's class path
rules.description: The running game loads a jar from outside the instance, the launcher's library and version folders, and the jar is not recognised as the launcher's own. Adding a jar to the class path is a way to inject code without using the mods folder.
rules.falsePositives: Custom launch scripts and some third-party launchers place jars elsewhere.
rules.limitations: Only the class path of the selected process is examined.

rules.name: Vanilla client jar does not match Mojang's published hash
rules.description: The SHA-1 of the client jar on the running game's class path differs from the hash Mojang publishes in the version manifest next to it, meaning the game code itself was modified.
rules.falsePositives: A corrupted download produces the same result; the launcher normally re-downloads mismatching files.
rules.limitations: Only versions whose manifest declares downloads.client.sha1 can be checked; launchers that store the manifest elsewhere are reported as not verifiable.

rules.name: Archive disguised as a different mod
rules.description: The file name claims a well-known mod (e.g. 'sodium-…jar') but the archive's own metadata declares a different, unrelated mod id.
rules.falsePositives: Repackaged or forked builds sometimes keep upstream file names.
rules.limitations: Only triggers for file names containing a known-mod id.

rules.name: Duplicate mod id across archives
rules.description: Two archives in the same mods folder declare the same mod id, which can indicate a swapped or disguised copy.
rules.falsePositives: Users often leave an old version next to an update.
rules.limitations: Mod loaders refuse to start with duplicates, so the configuration may never have run.

rules.name: Native executable embedded in archive
rules.description: The archive contains a Windows executable (PE) image. Executables hidden under non-library names or extensions are reported as strong indicators.
rules.falsePositives: Many legitimate mods ship native libraries (.dll) for audio codecs, voice chat, Discord presence or compression; those are inspected but not reported unless their strings match.
rules.limitations: Only PE images are recognised.

rules.name: Encrypted or non-standard class files in archive
rules.description: Entries named *.class do not start with the Java class-file magic (CAFEBABE). The JVM cannot load them directly, so the archive must decrypt them with its own class loader — a technique used to hide cheat code from string and class scanning.
rules.falsePositives: A handful of mods ship non-class data under a .class name by mistake; a single entry is reported as a weak indicator only.
rules.limitations: The encrypted content itself cannot be inspected; the finding is about the concealment technique.

rules.name: Unexpected executable inside the instance
rules.description: A Windows executable or DLL is stored inside the Minecraft instance outside its native-library folders and is not Authenticode-signed. Executables disguised with another extension are strong indicators.
rules.falsePositives: Some mods extract unsigned helper DLLs into the instance (e.g. Discord rich presence).
rules.limitations: Signed executables are listed in the inventory but not reported.

rules.name: Java agent entry point inside mod archive
rules.description: The archive's manifest declares Premain-Class/Agent-Class, so it can be attached to the JVM as an instrumentation agent and rewrite game classes at load time.
rules.falsePositives: A few legitimate developer tools ship agent manifests; normal gameplay mods do not need one.
rules.limitations: Detects capability, not use.

rules.name: JVM options injected through the game's environment
rules.description: The environment of the selected game process contains JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS / _JAVA_OPTIONS / JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with -javaagent or -agentpath, so the JVM loaded an agent that does not appear in the visible launch arguments.
rules.falsePositives: Rare developer setups (profilers, APM agents).
rules.limitations: Read from the selected process's own environment block; no other variable is collected.

rules.name: Java agent supplied in launch arguments
rules.description: The selected game process (or its launcher configuration inside the instance) uses -javaagent/-agentpath with an agent that is not the launcher's own.
rules.falsePositives: Profilers and some launchers use agents; launcher agents are allowlisted by their class content, not by path.
rules.limitations: Arguments are read from the selected process only.

rules.name: Game library does not match published hash
rules.description: A library jar on the running game's class path has a different SHA-1 than its version manifest declares.
rules.falsePositives: Interrupted downloads or manual library replacement by some launchers.
rules.limitations: Libraries without a declared hash cannot be checked.

rules.name: Instance folder redirected outside the instance
rules.description: A folder the game loads content from (mods, config, resourcepacks or shaderpacks) is a symbolic link or junction to a location outside the instance. The game loads the redirected content; hiding mods behind a link keeps them out of a casual look at the instance folder. The redirected folder is followed and inspected as part of the instance.
rules.falsePositives: Some players share one mods or resourcepacks folder between instances with links.
rules.limitations: Links inside other folders are not followed and are listed as not inspected.

rules.name: Instance log or crash report shows a known cheat client being loaded
rules.description: The mod list in a game log or crash report of the selected instance contains a mod id that belongs to a known cheat client.
rules.falsePositives: Log files can be copied from elsewhere, but this is uncommon.
rules.limitations: Shows the client was loaded by the game at the log's timestamp, not which server was joined.

rules.name: Mod loaded in a previous session is no longer present
rules.description: A log of the selected instance shows a mod being loaded that no longer exists in the instance's mods folder. Removing mods shortly before a screenshare is a common concealment technique.
rules.falsePositives: Users legitimately remove or update mods between sessions.
rules.limitations: Logs only list mod ids and versions, not file hashes.

rules.name: Cheat feature names present in game memory
rules.description: Several distinct cheat-feature names (e.g. KillAura, AimAssist, TriggerBot) were found as strings in the memory of the selected game process.
rules.falsePositives: Chat messages, server MOTDs or GUI text discussing cheats put the same words in memory. Treat as a lead only.
rules.limitations: Memory scanning is capped per process; absence proves nothing.

rules.name: Inconsistent mod metadata
rules.description: The mod metadata references entrypoint classes or mixin configurations that do not exist in the archive, or the archive declares no metadata while containing game-modifying classes.
rules.falsePositives: Broken builds and mods that rely on language adapters can produce the same pattern.
rules.limitations: Kotlin/Scala adapter entrypoints and nested archives are taken into account.

rules.name: Mods folder changed after the last game session
rules.description: A file in the instance's mods folder was modified or created after the instance's most recent game log was written.
rules.falsePositives: Installing or updating mods between sessions is normal.
rules.limitations: File timestamps can be altered.

rules.name: Archive impersonates a well-known mod
rules.description: The archive declares the mod id of a well-known mod, but contains none of the class packages every genuine build of that mod ships. Cheat clients adopt popular mod ids to blend into the mod list.
rules.falsePositives: Unofficial forks that were re-packaged under a new package name.
rules.limitations: Only mods with documented packages in the known-mods database are checked; archives verified on Modrinth are excluded.

rules.name: Cheat-module class structure in archive
rules.description: The archive contains classes named after several distinct cheat features (e.g. KillAura, AimAssist, Scaffold) organised like a hacked client's module system.
rules.falsePositives: A legitimate mod may contain one similarly named class (e.g. a 'Reach' attribute). Severity rises with the number of distinct high-signal names.
rules.limitations: Obfuscated clients rename classes and evade this heuristic.

rules.name: Java archive with a non-jar extension in mods folder
rules.description: A file in a mods folder is a Java archive but uses a different extension, which may hide it from casual inspection while some loaders/injectors still use it.
rules.falsePositives: Launchers disable mods by appending '.disabled'; those are reported separately as informational.
rules.limitations: Disabled archives are not loaded by the game.

rules.name: Heavily obfuscated mod archive
rules.description: Most class names in the archive are one or two characters long or use non-ASCII/confusable names, consistent with commercial obfuscation used by paid clients.
rules.falsePositives: Some legitimate closed-source mods are obfuscated (e.g. OptiFine-style distributions).
rules.limitations: Obfuscation is not proof of cheating.

rules.name: Executable disguised as a Java archive
rules.description: The file is a Windows executable that also contains a ZIP/JAR directory (or has data prepended to the archive). Such polyglot files can be loaded as a mod and run as a program.
rules.falsePositives: Self-extracting installers have the same structure but do not belong in a mods folder.
rules.limitations: Structure only; the executable part is string-scanned for injection indicators.

rules.name: File could not be inspected
rules.description: A relevant file of the instance could not be fully inspected (locked, unreadable, corrupt, encrypted entries or above the size limit). The scan cannot make a statement about its content.
rules.falsePositives: Not an accusation. Files in use by the game are normally still readable.
rules.limitations: Listed so the investigator knows exactly what was not examined.

rules.name: Unrecognised modification (manual review)
rules.description: A mod archive in the instance is not in the catalog of known mods and could not be verified against the Modrinth registry. Listed for manual review.
rules.falsePositives: Most unrecognised mods are legitimate niche or private mods.
rules.limitations: Listed for completeness; this is not an accusation.

rules.name: Unsigned native module loaded into the game
rules.description: The selected game process has a native DLL loaded from a user-writable location without a valid Authenticode signature and not matching known game natives (LWJGL, OpenAL, GLFW, JNA, voice-chat codecs).
rules.falsePositives: Overlays, shader tools and some legitimate mods load unsigned natives.
rules.limitations: Only the selected process is examined, at scan time.

rules.name: X-ray textures in resource pack
rules.description: The resource pack replaces common terrain blocks (stone, deepslate, dirt, netherrack…) with fully transparent textures or empty block models, which makes ores visible through terrain. Detected from the pack's content, so renaming the pack does not hide it.
rules.falsePositives: Some creative/map-making packs make blocks transparent deliberately.
rules.limitations: Shader-based X-ray and packs that only tint textures are not detected by this check.

rules.limitations: Targets old (1.7/1.8-era) injection clients; current releases are not covered.

rules.description: The binary imports CreateRemoteThread, the classic API for running code inside another process.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.
rules.limitations: Packed or encrypted binaries hide their imports; absence of these strings proves nothing.

rules.name: Remote memory allocation API
rules.description: The binary imports VirtualAllocEx, used to allocate memory inside another process.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.
rules.limitations: Packed or encrypted binaries hide their imports; absence of these strings proves nothing.

rules.name: Remote memory write API
rules.description: The binary imports WriteProcessMemory, used to write code or data into another process.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.

rules.name: Undocumented thread creation API
rules.description: The binary references NtCreateThreadEx, an undocumented API used by injectors to bypass CreateRemoteThread monitoring.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.
rules.limitations: Packed or encrypted binaries hide their imports; absence of these strings proves nothing.

rules.name: Attach to running Java VM from native code
rules.description: The binary calls JNI_GetCreatedJavaVMs, which native code injected into javaw.exe uses to obtain the game's JVM and load cheat classes into it.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.
rules.limitations: Packed or encrypted binaries hide their imports; absence of these strings proves nothing.

rules.name: JVM tool interface agent entry point
rules.description: The binary exports Agent_OnAttach, the entry point of a native JVMTI agent that can be attached to a running game.
rules.falsePositives: Each string has legitimate uses; only combinations are reported, and never as proof.
rules.limitations: Packed or encrypted binaries hide their imports; absence of these strings proves nothing.

rules.name: Freecam modification

rules.limitations: Server policy determines whether this is a violation. Presence on disk does not prove use on the server.

rules.name: X-ray modification (name/metadata)
rules.description: A mod whose id or name contains "xray" is installed. X-ray mods render ores and hidden blocks through terrain.
rules.falsePositives: Mods with xray in the name may be anti-xray tools for server owners, or utilities for singleplayer/creative.
rules.limitations: Name-based. Requires manual review of the mod.

rules.name: X-ray resource pack
rules.description: A resource pack whose name contains "xray" is present. X-ray texture packs make stone transparent so ores are visible.
rules.falsePositives: Pack names are user-controlled; a pack may be mis-named or unused.
rules.limitations: Only checks the pack file/folder name, not whether the pack was active.

rules.name: Tweakeroo (gameplay tweaks incl. freecam/fast placement)
rules.description: Tweakeroo is installed. It contains optional features (freecam, fast block placement) that many PvP servers prohibit.
rules.falsePositives: Tweakeroo is a popular, legitimate technical-play mod; most features are harmless.
rules.limitations: Cannot see which tweaks were enabled unless its config is reviewed manually.

rules.name: Item Scroller (inventory automation)
rules.description: Item Scroller automates inventory item movement and crafting.
rules.falsePositives: Widely allowed on survival servers; usually only prohibited in competitive PvP.
rules.limitations: Presence only.
